title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral (and often the following bolding asterisks) that begins an item in a numbered list, such as '4. **', '5.', '**10.', etc. It activates specifically on the ordinal token/punctuation marking a new list entry, regardless of the topic of the list (recipes, tips, rankings, categories, etc.) or the number's value. It does not activate on the textual content of the list item itself, on bullet points without numerals, or on numbers used in other contexts like dates, quantities, or in-sentence counting.

title: Chatbot follow-up probe: 'tell me more'
description: This latent fires specifically on the templated conversational-assistant phrase 'Can/Could you tell me more about...' (and close variants like 'a bit more about'), used to invite elaboration from the user in a therapeutic/advice-chatbot register. It activates most strongly on the exact canonical form 'Can you tell me more about what happened?' and similar short clarifying prompts, and more weakly on structurally similar but lexically varied follow-up questions that still open with this stem or a close paraphrase. It does not activate strongly on other clarifying or open-ended questions that lack the 'tell me more' construction, such as 'What's the context of this person...', 'Is there something specific...', or 'Would you like to talk about...', even though these serve a similar conversational function—indicating the latent is tuned to the specific surface phrasing rather than the general act of soliciting elaboration.

title: Interpersonal-conflict advice narration
description: This latent fires on sentences from advice/relationship-conflict responses (e.g., AITA/relationship-advice style text) that narrate, validate, or reframe a social situation — restating what someone did, assessing whether their behavior or another's was reasonable/unreasonable, reading social cues, or offering justification/empathy for feelings and actions. It activates on statements like 'X was being unreasonable,' 'it's understandable that you felt...,' 'if they start fidgeting or checking their phone, they may be ready to leave,' and second-person recaps of a scenario ('You were doing your thing, minding your own business'). It does not activate on neutral factual or instructional content unrelated to interpersonal judgment (e.g., measurements of Earth's diameter, generic list headers, or task instructions) unless framed as evaluating someone's social conduct or feelings within a conflict narrative.

title: Interpersonal advice-column reasoning
description: This latent fires on the characteristic rhetorical moves of advice/relationship-advice text: hedged psychological explanations for another person's behavior ("he might not realize/be aware..."), reminders of rights and boundaries ("you don't owe anyone an explanation"), suggested collaborative phrasings ("Can we find a way to..."), and evaluative or empathic framing statements about interpersonal conflicts (impact on relationships, responsibility, fairness, compromise). It activates on sentences that perform advice-giving discourse functions—empathetic speculation about others' motives, boundary-setting statements, suggested conversation openers, or listing potential pitfalls/considerations in a relationship or life-decision context—rather than on the specific topic (money, chores, dating, family) being discussed. It would not activate on purely factual, narrative, or technical sentences lacking this interpersonal-advice, motive-speculation, or boundary-affirming structure, even if they mention similar topics like relationships or money.

title: Illustrative example lists of everyday activities
description: This latent fires on short lists of concrete, mundane examples—favorite meals, movies, hobbies, small gifts, chores, casual conversation topics—typically offered as illustrative options after a general suggestion (often introduced by 'This could be,' 'such as,' 'like,' or presented as bullet points or quoted sample questions). It activates most strongly on the enumerated example items themselves (a meal, a movie, coffee, chores, a small gift) rather than on the surrounding advice-giving or reasoning. It does not activate on sentences that state facts, describe a specific past event, give a single non-list recommendation, or discuss abstract/relational reasoning without offering a set of casual, everyday alternative examples.

title: Speculative relational psychologizing (often as either/or questions)
description: This latent fires on text that speculates about another person's (or one's own) hidden emotions, motives, or intentions in an interpersonal/relationship context, frequently phrased as open or either/or questions ('Is he genuinely X, or is he Y?', 'Maybe she's feeling...', 'They might be worried about...'). It activates on hedged, hypothesis-generating language ('perhaps', 'maybe', 'might', 'is it possible that') used to probe why someone acted a certain way or how they feel, typically in advice-column or relationship-counseling style prose. It does not activate on flat factual statements, narrative description without psychological speculation, or direct assertions of feeling without the tentative/questioning framing (e.g., simple statements like 'He was upset' without any hedge or alternative possibility) -- the presence of uncertainty markers and dual/alternative possibilities about internal states is key, not merely discussing emotions or relationships.

title: Closing-remark reminder phrase
description: This latent fires on the discourse-marker word 'Remember' (and closely related closing phrases like 'Lastly,' or 'Ultimately, it's important to remember') that introduce a concluding piece of advice, especially in advice/relationship-counseling contexts. It activates most strongly on the bare cue word itself at the start of a sentence, before or as the reminder content unfolds, and generalizes to variants emphasizing final takeaways about communication, boundaries, self-care, or personal growth. It does not activate on advice sentences that lack this summarizing/reminder framing (e.g., direct suggestions like 'Set boundaries' or descriptive statements like 'It's essential to consider...') even when the topic is identical, since the key trigger is the rhetorical framing device signaling a wrap-up reminder rather than the advice content itself.

title: Empathetic interpersonal-advice hedging
description: This latent fires on sentences from advice/therapy-style text that interpret how someone's words or actions may have emotionally impacted another person, typically using hedged, speculative phrasing like 'might have contributed to,' 'may have made her feel,' 'could have been perceived as.' It also activates on related empathetic framing devices in relationship/conflict advice: acknowledging validity of feelings ('it's understandable,' 'it's reasonable'), evaluative judgments of behavior as inconsiderate/unhealthy/toxic, and exclamatory validation of the questioner's insight ('What a thoughtful question!'). It does not activate on neutral factual statements, procedural instructions/lists (e.g., 'contact the store manager'), or plain narrative facts without an interpersonal-emotional-impact framing, even within the same advice-column genre.

title: Validating/reassuring interpersonal advice
description: This latent fires on sentences from advice-giving or relationship-counseling text that validate, reassure, or affirm the reader's feelings, rights, or choices, and on related empathetic framing phrases (e.g., 'coming from a place of love and concern,' 'it's up to you to decide,' 'you're not wrong/bad for...', 'you have every right to...'). It activates on second-person statements that normalize emotions, grant permission, set boundaries, or acknowledge the difficulty of a situation, typically in the context of interpersonal, emotional, or relationship advice. It does not activate on purely factual, descriptive, or third-person narrative content (e.g., explanations of eclipses, procedural instructions, or plot summaries) unless it also contains this reassuring/validating second-person address, even if such sentences appear in the same document.

title: Rhetorical framing exclamation for a familiar dilemma
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic exclamatory openers that frame the upcoming discussion as a well-known type of problem or reaction—typically of the form '[The] age-old/classic/eternal + noun (dilemma/conundrum/debate/struggle/concern)!' or brief interjections like 'The irony!', 'Ah, yes!', 'A curious question!'. These sentences serve a discourse function: they signal recognition of a familiar situational category before advice or analysis follows, often in advice-column or AITA-style responses, and are almost always standalone, punchy, exclamation-marked phrases rather than full argumentative sentences. It is most strongly activated by the bare templated phrase itself (e.g., 'The age-old dilemma!' with no elaboration), and activates more weakly when the phrase is followed by a descriptive qualifier (e.g., 'of ice cream coupons'). It does NOT activate on full evaluative or advisory sentences that state a verdict or offer reasoning (e.g., 'You're not the asshole for...', 'I think you're being reasonable...'), even if they discuss similar dilemma-laden topics, nor on plain empathetic statements like 'I'm so sorry to hear that' that lack the 'age-old/classic' framing device.

title: Empathetic validation opener
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic exclamatory phrases that an assistant uses to affirm, validate, or empathize with the user's statement before (or instead of) substantive content—e.g. 'That's a great insight!', 'I totally understand!', 'That's so sweet!', 'What a profound insight!'. These are brief, high-affect, often exclamation-marked acknowledgments that praise an idea, validate a feeling, or express emotional resonance, typically standing as their own sentence/utterance rather than embedded in longer explanatory text. It activates most strongly on these terse validation formulas and less strongly on longer, more discursive empathetic or advisory sentences (e.g. multi-clause explanations of why a feeling is understandable, or hedged advice-giving sentences) which share the empathetic tone but lack the short, punchy affirmational structure. Sentences that give substantive advice, ask questions, or narrate a situation without an exclamatory validating frame do not trigger it.

title: Benefit-explaining sentence opener ('This can/will help...')
description: This latent fires on sentences that begin with a demonstrative pronoun ('This') followed by a modal verb of possibility ('can', 'will', 'could', 'might') and a verb like 'help', 'lead to', or 'create', introducing the positive (or occasionally negative) consequence of a previously described action or behavior. It activates most strongly on the templated pattern 'This can help you [verb phrase]' used in advice-giving text to justify a recommendation (e.g., staying focused, building confidence, reducing tension, strengthening relationships), and also fires somewhat on structurally similar consequence clauses like 'This could lead to frustration...' or 'This can create resentment...'. It does not activate on sentences describing the recommended action itself, on sentences with different subjects (e.g., 'A therapist can help...', 'They may be able to...'), or on general advice sentences that lack the initial 'This + modal + help/lead/create' clause structure.

title: Empathetic supportive-listener framing
description: This latent fires on formulaic assistant self-descriptions that position the speaker as a supportive, non-judgmental listener, typically phrased as 'I'm here to listen/help/support you' with variants offering advice, brainstorming, or a sympathetic ear. It activates most strongly on short, stock phrases that foreground emotional availability and willingness to help ('I'm here to listen and offer support', 'I'm here to help you navigate this'), and less strongly on longer sentences that still contain this supportive framing but add substantive content, caveats, or perspective-giving (e.g., 'I'm not a therapist, but...', 'I'm here to offer a neutral perspective and acknowledge...'). It would not activate on sentences that give actual advice, information, or judgments without this relational/supportive framing, nor on unrelated declarative or factual statements lacking the 'I'm here to...' empathetic-helper construction.

title: Validating-but-boundary-setting advice phrasing
description: This latent fires on advice-column style sentences that validate someone's feelings, actions, or circumstances ('it's essential to acknowledge...', 'your emotions are valid', 'it's not your fault') while often pairing that validation with a boundary, caveat, or reminder to also consider another perspective ('even if it's uncomfortable', 'but it's also important to consider...'). It activates strongly on formulaic empathetic-therapeutic phrasing built around 'it's [adjective/essential/important] to...' or 'X is valid/natural/normal', typically appearing in relationship, emotional, or interpersonal advice contexts, and often on isolated clause fragments beginning with 'It's'. It does not activate on purely factual, descriptive, or narrative sentences lacking this validating-advisory register, nor on direct questions, instructions unrelated to emotional acknowledgment, or sentences that state opinions without the characteristic 'it's important/essential/valid' hedging-affirmation structure.

title: Cliché framing of a dilemma
description: This latent fires on stock exclamatory phrases that introduce or label a relatable dilemma/debate, such as 'The age-old dilemma!', 'The classic conundrum!', or 'The eternal question!', typically used as a rhetorical opener before discussing an interpersonal or everyday conflict (e.g., etiquette, boundaries, roommate/family drama). It activates most strongly on the bare formulaic phrase itself (often followed by an exclamation point), especially variants using 'age-old,' 'eternal,' or 'classic' plus a noun like dilemma/conundrum/question/debate, sometimes with a brief topic tag appended. It does not activate on the substantive advice, reasoning, or solutions that follow such openers (e.g., lists of steps, suggestions to communicate or seek therapy), nor on other rhetorical exclamations that don't use this specific 'stock dilemma-naming' template (e.g., 'What an insightful realization!'), indicating the latent tracks this particular clichéd framing device rather than the topic or content of the dilemma discussed.

title: Advice-column relational reasoning
description: This latent fires on text characteristic of advice/relationship-advice responses: statements that interpret someone's interpersonal situation, validate or reframe their feelings, suggest alternative approaches they 'could have' taken, or pose clarifying questions about motives, relationships, and decisions ('Who are she and them?', 'Was it X or Y?', 'You could have approached this more tactfully'). It activates on sentences offering reassurance, suggesting communication strategies, listing options/considerations in advice contexts, and hypothesizing about others' intentions or feelings in social conflicts. It does not activate on purely factual, technical, or descriptive statements unrelated to interpersonal advice-giving (e.g., nutritional facts, tax definitions, or market listings), even though a few such sentences appear here because they co-occur with other advice-latent content in the same passage; the core driver is the advice-column reasoning pattern, not the topic itself.

title: Evaluative verdict on a person's reaction/behavior
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic evaluative statements that pass judgment on a specific person's behavior or reaction, typically in the pattern [Possessive noun]'s [reaction/behavior] was [evaluative adjective], e.g. 'unacceptable,' 'unreasonable,' 'unprofessional,' 'understandable,' or 'disproportionate.' It activates most strongly on the clearest, most templatic verdict sentences (often bolded headers in advice-column-style responses) that name a specific party (dad, mom, sister, employer, officer, etc.) and assign a clear moral/behavioral judgment to their conduct, whether negative (unacceptable, hurtful, aggressive) or occasionally positive/mitigating (understandable, excellent, reasonable). It activates more weakly on sentences that discuss reactions/behavior but embed the judgment within longer explanatory or hedged context, or that describe feelings/intentions/causes rather than delivering a direct evaluative verdict on someone's conduct. It would not fire on purely descriptive or narrative sentences that report events without assigning an evaluative label to a person's behavior (e.g., factual statements, requests, or background context lacking a judgment word).

title: Interpersonal-advice relational framing
description: This latent fires on language from relationship/advice-column style text that frames a situation in terms of emotional needs, boundaries, inclusion, validation, or being 'aware of impact on others' — the therapeutic/mediation register used to interpret someone's behavior or suggest a compromise. It activates on sentences hypothesizing others' unconscious motives ('they might not be aware of the impact...'), affirming feelings/boundaries ('that's a reasonable boundary', 'you deserve to feel included'), and phrases about communicating needs, seeking compromise, or feeling valued/included/supported. It also fires on formulaic hedges like 'there's no one-size-fits-all solution' and on invitations to open dialogue ('Can we find a way to...?'). It does not activate on purely factual, technical, or narrative sentences lacking this relational/advice framing (e.g., travel tips, economic data, historical quotes) even if topically adjacent, unless they too invoke feelings, inclusion, or interpersonal negotiation.

title: Polite request/question scripts in quoted speech
description: This latent fires on modeled conversational utterances—typically quoted, suggested phrasings someone could say to another person—that take the form of polite requests, proposals, or questions ('Can we...?', 'Would you be willing to...?', 'Could we...?', 'What do you think...?'). It activates most strongly on short, self-contained interrogative or softly-worded request sentences that end in quotation marks, often examples of scripted dialogue for negotiating boundaries, making plans, or asking permission in interpersonal advice contexts. It does not activate (or activates weakly) on declarative statements, explanations of advice ('Use "I" statements...'), meta-commentary about communication strategies, or first-person emotional disclosures that are not phrased as a direct question/request to the other person—i.e., the distinguishing feature is the grammatical form of a polite, second-person-directed question/request rather than the topic of interpersonal conflict or communication advice itself.

title: Listicle items of practical options and requirements
description: This latent fires on individual entries within enumerated, advice-style lists that present concrete options, resources, providers, or bureaucratic requirements (e.g., insurance plans, licensing steps, discount programs, service providers, waiting periods), frequently formatted as a bolded term or heading followed by a colon and an explanatory clause. It activates most strongly on sentences that name a specific category or entity (e.g., 'Manufacturer discounts**:', 'Google**:', 'HealthCare.gov**:') and then give a factual, informational elaboration about eligibility, cost, coverage, or procedure. It does not activate on narrative, emotional, or interpersonal reasoning sentences (e.g., advice about relationships, feelings, or personal conflicts) even when they appear in similarly structured lists, nor on plain declarative facts lacking the 'option/requirement item' framing typical of how-to or resource-listing content.

title: AITA verdict phrasing
description: This latent fires on the stock verdict/question templates used in 'Am I the Asshole' (AITA) style moral-judgment discourse, especially the formulaic phrase 'you're/you are not the asshole (in this situation)' and its close variants ('AITA?', 'am I the asshole?', 'NTA', 'you would not be the asshole'). It activates most strongly on short, canonical, near-verbatim instances of this template, including question forms ('So, AITA?', 'Are you the asshole?') and negated verdict forms, and activates more weakly on longer sentences that embed similar verdict language within hedged or elaborated reasoning (e.g., 'Overall, while you could have handled things better, I don't think you're the asshole'). It would not activate on general moral or advice-giving sentences that don't use this specific 'asshole/AH/NTA/YTA' verdict framing, such as generic reassurances ('you're not alone'), unrelated advice ('have an open conversation with your husband'), or judgments phrased without the asshole terminology at all.

title: Affirming validation ('you deserve...') reassurance
description: This latent fires on second-person affirming statements that validate the reader's worth, feelings, or rights, typically using formulas like 'you deserve to be...', 'you are entitled to...', or 'you are worthy of...' followed by respect, love, kindness, safety, or well-being. It activates most strongly on short, formulaic reassurance sentences addressed directly to 'you' that assert entitlement or deservingness, often used as a supportive closing line in advice-giving text (e.g., therapeutic, relationship, or workplace advice). It is weaker or inactive on sentences that give concrete advice, describe actions, or discuss third parties or general principles (e.g., 'it's important to respect boundaries' or 'she is strong and capable') without the direct 'you deserve/are entitled/worthy' validating address, even though such sentences may share the theme of respect or self-care.

title: Congratulatory/welcoming opener phrase
description: This latent fires on formulaic opening phrases that congratulate or welcome the reader, typically as a stock conversational courtesy at the start of a response (e.g., 'Congratulations on your X!', 'Welcome to the community!', 'Welcome to Reddit!'). It activates most strongly on short, templated exclamations naming a specific life event (marriage, pregnancy, new job, move, graduation) or generic welcome/greeting formulas, including variants prefixed with 'Firstly,'. It activates more weakly but still noticeably on longer sentences that embed similar congratulatory praise within advice-giving text (e.g., 'congratulations on taking the first step toward...'), but does not activate on sentences that merely give advice, express empathy, or discuss the topic (e.g., pregnancy, moving, jobs) without the ritualized congratulate/welcome phrasing itself.

title: Advice-list header transition
description: This latent fires on the introductory phrase that precedes a numbered or bulleted list of suggestions, tips, or steps in advice-giving text (e.g., 'Here are some suggestions:', 'Some potential steps you could take:', 'Additional tips for...'), often immediately followed by '1.' or a bolded list item. It activates specifically on the transitional sentence or header that frames upcoming enumerated advice, rather than on the advice content itself, and is strongest when this header is short, formulaic, and directly abuts the list markup. It does not activate on the substantive advice items themselves, on narrative or explanatory sentences without a following list, or on general commentary/opinion sentences (e.g., statements of concern, empathy, or analysis) that lack this list-introducing structure.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral (and often trailing punctuation or bold markdown asterisks) that marks the start of an item in an enumerated or numbered list, especially early list items like '2.' or '3.' in a sequence. It activates on the digit-plus-period token pattern itself, regardless of what topic the list is about, and is largely indifferent to the surrounding content. It does not activate on prose sentences, bullet points using dashes or asterisks alone without numerals, or on the list's introductory header line, nor strongly on higher numbers deep into long lists (activation is concentrated on low ordinal markers like 2 and 3). It is a structural/formatting latent tracking numbered-list enumeration syntax rather than semantic content.

title: Transitional lead-in before a list
description: This latent fires on short introductory phrases that immediately precede a numbered or bulleted list, such as 'Here's why:', 'Here's a breakdown:', 'You:', or 'Let's break it down:'. It activates specifically at the structural transition point where the text signals that enumerated reasons, steps, or points are about to follow, often right before a '1.' marker. It is strongest on the most formulaic, minimal-content lead-ins ('Here's why:') and weaker but still active on more varied or elaborated transitional phrases ('Now, let's explore alternative approaches:', 'Here are a few suggestions that might help you address the issue:'). It does not activate on the actual list content, on standalone rhetorical questions without a following list ('What do you think?'), or on full sentences that make substantive claims rather than serving as a structural pivot into enumeration.

title: Empathetic advice validation
description: This latent fires on the rhetorical moves typical of therapeutic or interpersonal-advice writing: validating the reader's feelings or rights ('you deserve...', 'you're entitled to...'), urging balance or compromise between competing needs ('find a balance between X and Y'), and posing reflective, clarifying questions ('Are you...?', 'What...?', 'Is it...?') that prompt the person to examine their motives or situation. It activates on reassuring, non-judgmental framings that acknowledge both sides of a conflict, soften criticism, or encourage empathy and self-reflection, often in the context of relationship, family, or personal-conduct advice. It does not activate on purely factual, descriptive, or narrative statements lacking this validating/reflective/balancing stance (e.g., plain factual claims about geography or mechanics), even if they share topical overlap with advice-like content.

title: Validating/advice-giving in relationship dilemmas
description: This latent fires on sentences from advice-column-style responses to interpersonal relationship problems (romantic partners, family, in-laws, friends, roommates), particularly ones that validate the reader's feelings, assign or excuse blame, explain another person's possible motivations, or offer gentle reassurance and suggestions ('You're not alone in feeling...', 'That doesn't excuse...', 'Maybe they were having a bad day', 'It's completely reasonable to want...'). It captures the empathetic, reasoning-through-a-conflict register of advice/therapy-style text that interprets behavior, assesses fairness, and reassures someone about their feelings or actions in a dispute. It does not activate on neutral factual statements, narrow lists/instructions unrelated to relational judgment, or purely descriptive sentences lacking an evaluative or validating stance toward a person's feelings or conduct.

title: Empathetic advice-column validation
description: This latent fires on sentences from advice/AITA-style responses that directly address 'you' (the letter-writer) with validating, reassuring, or reframing commentary about their feelings, actions, or situation—e.g. 'You have every right to be upset,' 'It's okay to grieve,' 'That being said, it's also not entirely your fault.' It activates on second-person evaluative statements that acknowledge the person's perspective, assign or mitigate blame, encourage self-reflection ('identify the root cause of...'), or offer reassurance and permission ('you don't have to have it all figured out'), typically in the register of relationship/interpersonal advice responses. It also fires on transitional hedges like 'That being said,' 'However,' or 'While this might be true' that soften or qualify judgments in this advice context. It does not activate on neutral factual statements, third-person narration without direct address, generic instructions unrelated to emotional/interpersonal validation, or isolated list markers and numbers unless attached to such advice-giving language.

title: Imperative relationship-advice directives
description: This latent fires on second-person imperative or advisory sentences that coach the reader through interpersonal/emotional situations — telling them to communicate, be patient, reflect, ask questions, set boundaries, or acknowledge feelings. It activates on advice-column/therapy-style directives ("Be patient and understanding," "Take time to reflect," "Ask questions and listen actively"), empathetic openers ("I'm so sorry to hear about..."), and numbered list markers ("3.") that structure such advice, as well as fragments that are clearly part of this advice-giving register. It does not activate on purely factual, narrative, or descriptive statements that lack a coaching/interpersonal-guidance framing, nor on technical or unrelated imperative instructions (e.g. recipe steps or coding commands) that don't concern emotional/relational conduct.
